title: Aerospace / jet-engine superalloy chain
thesis: A jet engine's bottleneck is not the ore. Chile's rhenium is a copper by-product; China makes most titanium sponge but almost none of it is aerospace-qualified; single-crystal blade casting is held by a few firms; and three Western groups build nearly every large engine. Each stage downstream is MORE concentrated than the mine.

data.note: Rhenium is recovered as a by-product of molybdenum from porphyry copper ores — no mine operates for rhenium itself, so supply cannot be scaled independently of copper.

mine_leaders.basis: share of world MINE production (porphyry copper by-product)

data.reading: The metal that makes single-crystal turbine blades possible is a trace by-product of copper mining, ~55% from Chile. It is a chokepoint by scarcity and by-product coupling, not by refining.

data.world_sponge_note: China dominates titanium-sponge PRODUCTION (~71% of world output in 2024), but most Chinese sponge is not qualified for critical aerospace use.

aerospace_qualified.note: Aerospace-grade sponge is a narrow, allied subset of total production. The premium/qualified supply comes from Japan, Russia and Kazakhstan — not from the world's largest producer.

us_import_reliance.note: The United States has NO domestic titanium-sponge production and imports it.

data.reading: The sponge chokepoint is not tonnage — China leads that — it is QUALIFICATION. Aerospace runs on a narrow allied base (Japan above all), which is why a production-share map misreads the risk.

data.note: Casting nickel-superalloy single-crystal blades (directional solidification, hafnium/rhenium-bearing) is a low-yield, capital- and know-how-intensive stage held by a handful of firms and engine OEMs.
data.structure: Concentrated among specialist casters (e.g. Precision Castparts, Doncasters) and the OEMs' own foundries, in the United States, United Kingdom, France and Japan; China is developing capability. No public country-production series exists for this stage — company control is the right lens.
data.reading: This is the classic 'the refiner is not the source' stage: even with the ore and the sponge, the blade-casting capability is the true bottleneck, and it is measured in firms, not countries.

overall_oem_share.oem: GE Aerospace (incl. CFM JV with Safran)

data.segment_note: Narrow-body: CFM (GE+Safran) holds >60%, Pratt & Whitney ~35%. Wide-body: GE and Rolls-Royce split the field (RR strong on Trent-powered twins).
data.reading: The finished machine is the most concentrated stage of all — three Western groups build essentially every large commercial jet engine. The chokepoint has walked all the way downstream to the assembler.
